To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
We have developed a mouse model that expresses a human/mouse chimera of the CD3e receptor, which allows for in vivo evaluation of the activity of BiTE(r).

we have developed a genetically-engineered mouse model that enables the assessment of in vivo mechanisms regulating therapeutic activity of bi-specific T cell engager molecules in immunocomproment mice expressing a human/mouse chimera CD3 receptor.
1) We developed a genetically engineered huCD3 mouse model in which human CD3e was expressed in place of the endogenous CD3e gene.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design, synthesis and evaluation of new anticancer agents.
the development and application of novel methods for studying and controlling the dynamics of biological processes at the single cell level.
the development of novel methods for the synthesis of heterocyclic compounds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
BiTE® molecules have been shown to induce redirected T cell-mediated cytotoxicity and T cell-dependent cytokine production, and to induce tumor cell lysis in vitro and in vivo.

BiTE(r)s can induce potent antitumor responses in immunocompetant mice expressing a chimearic huCD3e receptor and can be combined with PD1 inhibitors to eradicate tumors that do not have T cell infiltration.
BiTE(r)-mediated tumor eradication requires a sufficient number of tumor-infiltrating CD3e-expressing T cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
BiTE molecules are effective in immunocompetant mice and the efficacy correlates with the number of T cells.

we have developed a genetically modified mouse expressing a chimerically humanized CD3 receptor that is recognized by BiTE molecules and have characterized the in vitro and in vivo activity of BiTE molecules in this model.
BiTEs are effective against solid tumors and that their efficacy is dependent on T cell infiltration and T cell activation, but not T cell number.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the huCD3e mouse provides a robust platform for the study of BiTE(r)s and other T cell engaging agents in the immunocompetent setting.

BiTE molecules can be used as an immunotherapeutic in vivo in immunocompetant mice, but the efficacy is dependent upon a number of factors, including the tumor model, dose, and T cell infiltration into the tumor.
BiTE molecules can be effective in the absence of pre-activation of endogenous T cell.
